explain.say: Follow 100 units of fuel into a combined heat and power plant, or CHP. About 35 come out as electricity, a little less than a power-only station, because the steam or exhaust is let out while still usefully hot.

faq.q: How much electricity does a CHP plant make?
faq.a: Typically 25 to 40 percent of the fuel's energy becomes electricity. Taking heat out at a useful temperature means the steam or engine exhaust leaves warmer, so slightly less electricity is made than in a power-only station.

faq.q: Where does the heat from CHP go?
faq.a: It heats water or makes steam for nearby users: district heating networks, hospitals, universities, greenhouses, and factories such as paper mills and chemical works that need lots of heat.
asks: Who uses the heat from a CHP plant?

faq.q: Why can't CHP use all the heat?
faq.a: Some heat is too cool to be useful, and flue gases must stay warm enough to rise up the chimney without forming acid. Pipes and machinery also lose a little heat.
asks: Where is energy still lost in CHP?

faq.a: Heat cannot travel far without cooling and costly pipes, so a CHP plant needs customers close by who want heat all year. In summer, when little heating is needed, much of the heat may have nowhere to go.
asks: What are the downsides of CHP?

faq.a: Natural gas engines and turbines are most common, but CHP can also burn biomass, biogas or waste. Some fuel cells and nuclear plants have supplied heat as well as electricity.

facts: Combined heat and power plants can use around 75 to 80 percent or more of their fuel's energy.
Combined heat and power is also called cogeneration.

quiz.why: CHP puts the heat a normal station throws away to good use, so far more of the fuel's energy is useful.

wrong.1: The gain comes from using the heat, not from hotter burning.
wrong.2: CHP still burns fuel; it just wastes less of it.
